lines.text: Driving is a privilege, not a right.
Violations can cost that privilege.

narration.text: Welcome to the first part of the New Jersey lesson on driving privileges and penalties. The manual opens with one key idea: driving is a privilege rather than a right. That single word, privilege, explains everything else in this lesson. Because it is a privilege, state law allows or requires suspension for certain violations, and that suspension can come on top of possible fines and imprisonment. In this unit you will learn the grounds for losing the privilege, who decides the suspensions that are not mandatory, when a problem driver can be re-examined, what makes someone a habitual offender, and how unpaid child support can reach your license.

lines.text: State law allows or requires suspension.
Suspension can stack on fines and imprisonment.

narration.text: Start with the difference between a right and a privilege. The manual is clear that driving in New Jersey is a privilege rather than a right, which is why the state can take it away. For certain violations, state law allows a suspension, and for others it requires one. Either way, the suspension does not replace other penalties. It can come on top of possible fines and imprisonment. So when you read about a penalty later in this lesson, remember that a fine, jail time and a suspension can all be part of the same outcome. Keeping that stacking idea in mind makes the rest of the penalty rules easier to follow and easier to remember.

lines.text: Unanswered or unpaid parking tickets.
No proof of insurance, driving while suspended.
Disqualification, drug or alcohol use, violations.
Fatal crash fault, ignored MVC notice.

narration.text: What can cost you the privilege? Some grounds are paperwork problems: unanswered or unpaid parking tickets, no proof of insurance and ignoring an MVC notice. Some are about the driver: a physical or mental disqualification, or drug or alcohol use. Others come from the road: traffic violations, driving while suspended and fault in a fatal crash. Notice how ordinary some of these are, since an unpaid parking ticket sits on the same list as fault in a fatal crash. The reach goes beyond the road, too. Owing six months or more of child support or court-ordered health coverage can lead to a court-ordered suspension of both driver and professional licenses.

lines.text: Some suspensions are not mandatory.
Chief Administrator or courts decide case by case.
A problem driver may be re-examined.

narration.text: Not every suspension is automatic. The manual says some suspensions are not mandatory, and those are decided case by case by the MVC Chief Administrator or the courts. That means the outcome can differ from one driver to the next. The Chief Administrator also has another tool. For a problem driver, the MVC Chief Administrator may order a re-examination to help decide whether to suspend driving privileges. Think of the re-examination as information gathering. It does not decide the outcome on its own; it helps inform the decision. So the two ideas fit together: some suspensions are judgment calls, and a re-examination can feed into that judgment.

lines.text: Three suspensions within three years.
Count suspensions, not tickets.

narration.text: Here is a detail that is easy to blur. A habitual offender is a driver whose license has been suspended three times within three years. Two parts of that definition matter. First, the count is suspensions, not tickets or violations, so a driver with tickets but no suspensions does not fit this definition. Second, the three suspensions must fall within three years. The number three appears twice, which makes it easy to remember but also easy to garble. Say it as three suspensions in three years. Later in this lesson you will see that driving while suspended as a habitual offender carries tougher penalties than an ordinary suspension, so the label matters.

lines.text: Three suspensions within three years.
What label applies?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: Jesse's license has been suspended three times within three years, and Jesse also has an unpaid parking ticket sitting in a drawer. What label does the manual give Jesse, and is the parking ticket a problem? Work it out before reading on. Jesse is a habitual offender, because that term means a driver whose license has been suspended three times within three years. The parking ticket matters too, since unanswered or unpaid parking tickets are on the list of grounds for losing the privilege. Driving is a privilege, and both the suspension record and the unpaid ticket can put it at risk.

lines.text: Driving is a privilege.
Know the grounds for suspension.
Three suspensions in three years: habitual offender.
Unpaid child support can cost licenses.

narration.text: Let us pull this unit together. Driving is a privilege rather than a right, and state law allows or requires suspension for certain violations, on top of possible fines and imprisonment. The grounds range from unpaid parking tickets and missing proof of insurance to fault in a fatal crash. Some suspensions are decided case by case by the MVC Chief Administrator or the courts, and a problem driver may be re-examined to help with that decision. Three suspensions within three years make a habitual offender. Finally, owing six months or more of child support or court-ordered health coverage can lead to a court-ordered suspension of both driver and professional licenses.

lines.text: Twenty-one to buy, possess or drink.
Underage penalties reach the license.

narration.text: This unit covers what New Jersey does when someone under twenty-one is caught with alcohol. The rule starts with an age: in New Jersey a person must be at least twenty-one to buy, possess or drink alcohol. The rule also reaches the adults around them, because adults who supply alcohol to underage people face serious consequences too. From there, the manual sets out penalties that can touch a young person's license even before they have one. You will learn the fine for underage buying or drinking where alcohol is sold, when a suspension begins for someone not yet licensed, and what an underage first offense with a low BAC brings.

lines.text: Under twenty-one at a licensed place.
Possible five hundred dollar fine.
License can be lost for a time.

narration.text: Picture a person under twenty-one ordering a drink at a place where alcohol is licensed for sale. The manual says that person may be fined five hundred dollars and lose their license for a time. Two penalties can apply together here: money and the license. Notice that this rule is about buying or drinking at a licensed place. It is separate from the BAC-based underage offense you will see shortly, which has its own suspension range. Also remember the other side of the counter. Adults who supply alcohol to underage people face serious consequences too, so the law does not place all of the responsibility on the young person alone.

lines.text: Suspension starts at first eligibility.
Education or treatment may be required.

narration.text: What if the underage person does not have a license yet? You might think a suspension means nothing to someone with no license to suspend. The manual closes that gap. If the underage person has no license yet, the suspension begins on the date they first become eligible for one. In other words, the penalty waits for them. On top of that, an alcohol education or treatment program may be required. So a young person who is caught before getting a license can still face a delay in getting one, plus a program to complete. The lesson is simple: having no license does not put a young person outside the reach of these penalties.

lines.text: Underage range: zero point zero one up to under zero point zero eight.
Adult first DUI starts at zero point zero eight.
Suspension: thirty to ninety days.

narration.text: Here is the trap. It is tempting to anchor on the adult number, zero point zero eight percent, and assume anything under it carries no penalty. For an underage driver, that is not how it works. An underage first offense covers a BAC from zero point zero one up to under zero point zero eight percent, and it brings a license suspension of thirty to ninety days. The suspension starts on the later of eligibility or conviction. Compare that with an adult first DUI, which starts at a BAC of zero point zero eight percent. So the underage range sits entirely below the adult line. If a question gives an underage driver a BAC under the adult limit, do not assume there is no penalty.

lines.text: Underage, BAC in the underage range.

What suspension applies, and what else comes with it? Work it out before reading on. The license is suspended thirty to ninety days, starting on the later of eligibility or conviction. The offense also brings fifteen to thirty days of community service, plus either an IDRC or an alcohol education and highway safety program. Keep the two ranges apart: thirty to ninety days is the suspension, and fifteen to thirty days is the community service. Say them in that order to keep them straight.

A person under twenty-one who buys or drinks where alcohol is licensed for sale may be fined five hundred dollars and lose their license for a time. With no license yet, the suspension begins on the date of first eligibility, and an education or treatment program may be required. An underage first offense with a BAC from zero point zero one up to under zero point zero eight percent brings thirty to ninety days of suspension, fifteen to thirty days of community service and an IDRC or education program.

title.text: First DUI fines and the IDRC

why_how.text: The first-DUI fine depends on BAC: two hundred fifty to four hundred dollars under zero point one zero percent, three hundred to five hundred at or above it.
Anyone charged with an alcohol-related traffic offense is detained at an IDRC, where education and a treatment evaluation take place.
First- and third-time offenders use their county IDRC, while second-time offenders go to one of three regional centers.

result.text: Lee owes a three hundred to five hundred dollar fine plus the yearly surcharge, and as a first offender is detained at the county IDRC.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a second offender goes back to the same county IDRC used the first time.

correction.text: Second-time offenders go to one of three regional IDRCs; the county centers serve first- and third-time offenders.

memory_support.text: Bigger BAC, bigger fine; odd offenses stay local.

rationale.text: First- and third-time offenders use their county IDRC, while second-time offenders go to one of three regional centers.

title.text: The cost of a first DUI

lines.text: Two first-DUI fine tiers.
Surcharges and IDRC charges add up.

narration.text: This unit is about what a first DUI costs in New Jersey, and the answer has several layers. The fine depends on the BAC, with one range for a BAC of zero point zero eight percent but under zero point one zero percent, and a higher range at zero point one zero percent or more. On top of the fine comes an annual surcharge, and then there is the IDRC, where offenders are detained and charged for the program. You will also learn which IDRC an offender goes to, which depends on whether it is a first, second or third offense, and what happens when an evaluation shows that someone needs treatment before getting licensed again.

lines.text: BAC zero point zero eight to under zero point one zero.
Fine: two hundred fifty to four hundred dollars.
Twelve to forty-eight hours at an IDRC.
Up to thirty days in jail.

narration.text: Start with the lower tier. For a first DUI with a BAC of zero point zero eight percent but under zero point one zero percent, the fine is two hundred fifty to four hundred dollars. That is not the whole penalty. The same offense brings twelve to forty-eight hours at an IDRC and up to thirty days in jail. So even at the bottom of the adult range, a first DUI can mean a fine, time at an IDRC and possible jail together. Hold on to the fine range of two hundred fifty to four hundred dollars, because the next slide raises it, and the two ranges overlap enough that they are easy to swap if you only remember one of them.

lines.text: BAC zero point one zero or higher.
Fine rises to three hundred to five hundred.
Higher BAC means a higher range.

narration.text: Now the higher tier. For a first DUI with a BAC of zero point one zero percent or higher, the fine rises to three hundred to five hundred dollars. Put the two side by side. A first DUI between zero point zero eight and under zero point one zero percent is fined two hundred fifty to four hundred dollars, while a first DUI at zero point one zero percent or more is fined three hundred to five hundred dollars. Both the bottom and the top of the range move up with the higher BAC. A simple way to keep them straight is to tie the bigger numbers to the bigger BAC. At zero point one zero or more, reach for three hundred to five hundred.

lines.text: Surcharge: one thousand dollars a year, three years.
IDRC: two hundred sixty-four dollars for twelve hours.
Three hundred twenty-one dollars for forty-eight hours.

narration.text: The fine is only one cost. A first DUI offense also carries an annual surcharge of one thousand dollars for three years. That surcharge is separate from the fine, and it repeats each year for three years. Then there is the IDRC. The IDRC charges two hundred sixty-four dollars when the program lasts twelve hours and three hundred twenty-one dollars when it lasts forty-eight hours. Recall that the lower-tier first DUI brings twelve to forty-eight hours at an IDRC, so those two charges match the two ends of that range. When you add the fine, the yearly surcharge and the IDRC charge together, a first DUI costs far more than the fine alone.

lines.text: Anyone charged is detained at an IDRC.
Education program and treatment evaluation.
Treatment: at least sixteen weeks.
Participation is a condition for relicensing.

narration.text: What happens at an IDRC? Anyone charged with an alcohol-related traffic offense must be detained at an IDRC. While there, offenders take an alcohol and highway safety education program and are evaluated for treatment needs. That evaluation can lead somewhere. Offenders found to need treatment are referred for a program of at least sixteen weeks, and satisfactory participation is a condition for getting licensed again. So the IDRC is more than a place to wait. It is where education happens and where a treatment need is identified, and that treatment can stand between an offender and a new license. Detention, education, evaluation, then treatment if needed.

lines.text: Twenty-one counties, each with an IDRC.
First and third offenders: county IDRC.
Second offenders: one of three regional IDRCs.

narration.text: Here is a pattern that trips people up. Each of New Jersey's twenty-one counties has an IDRC, and those county centers serve first-time and third-time offenders. Second-time offenders go somewhere else: one of three regional IDRCs. You might expect the centers to line up in order, with first offenders in one place and all repeat offenders in another, but the manual splits them as first and third at the county, second at the regional center. One way to remember it is that odd numbers stay local and the even number travels. When a question names a second offense, the answer is a regional IDRC. When it names a first or third offense, it is the county IDRC.

lines.text: Second offense: which IDRC?
First DUI: what yearly surcharge?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: Sam is facing a second alcohol offense, and Sam's friend Lee has just been convicted of a first DUI. Where will Sam be detained, and what yearly surcharge does Lee's first DUI carry? Work it out before reading on. Sam goes to one of the three regional IDRCs, because second-time offenders are not detained at the county center. Lee's first DUI carries an annual surcharge of one thousand dollars for three years, on top of the fine. If Lee's BAC was zero point zero eight but under zero point one zero percent, the fine is two hundred fifty to four hundred dollars, and at zero point one zero or more it is three hundred to five hundred.

lines.text: Lower tier: two hundred fifty to four hundred.
Higher tier: three hundred to five hundred.
Plus one thousand dollars a year, three years.
County IDRC for first and third offenders.

narration.text: Let us review. At a BAC of zero point zero eight but under zero point one zero percent, a first DUI is fined two hundred fifty to four hundred dollars, with twelve to forty-eight hours at an IDRC and up to thirty days in jail. At zero point one zero or more, the fine is three hundred to five hundred dollars. Add a surcharge of one thousand dollars a year for three years. The IDRC charges two hundred sixty-four dollars for twelve hours or three hundred twenty-one for forty-eight. Anyone charged is detained at an IDRC, first and third offenders at the county center and second offenders regionally, and needed treatment lasts at least sixteen weeks.

why_how.text: Under implied consent, driving on New Jersey roads already counts as agreeing to a breath test after an arrest for intoxicated driving.
Refusing does not avoid penalties: it brings detention, a hospital visit and a yearly surcharge of its own.

reasoning.text: Driving on New Jersey roads meant agreeing to the test, so the refusal leads to detention and a hospital where blood may be drawn.

result.text: Alex owes one thousand dollars a year for three years and, on a first-offense refusal conviction, cannot drive until an interlock is installed.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking that refusing the breath test avoids the costs of a DUI.

correction.text: Refusal carries a surcharge of one thousand dollars a year for three years, the same as a first DUI.

prompt.text: Alex is arrested for intoxicated driving and refuses the breath test. Where is Alex taken?

title.text: Implied consent on New Jersey roads

lines.text: Driving here means agreeing to a breath test.
Refusing has its own penalties.

narration.text: This unit covers the breath test and what happens if a driver refuses it. New Jersey has an implied consent law, and it changes how you should think about the test. You do not agree to the breath test at the roadside. Under the implied consent law, simply driving on New Jersey roads means agreeing to a breath test by police or hospital staff after an arrest for intoxicated driving. From there, the manual explains what happens to a driver who refuses, the surcharge that refusing carries, and how a refusal conviction tied to a first offense keeps a driver off the road until an ignition interlock device is installed.

lines.text: Agreement comes from driving on New Jersey roads.
Test by police or hospital staff.
Applies after an arrest for intoxicated driving.

narration.text: Let us slow down on implied consent. Under this law, the agreement is not something a driver signs at the roadside. It comes from the act of driving. By driving on New Jersey roads, a driver has already agreed to a breath test by police or hospital staff after an arrest for intoxicated driving. Three pieces are worth remembering. The agreement comes from driving on New Jersey roads. The test can be given by police or by hospital staff. And it applies after an arrest for intoxicated driving. So when an arrested driver says they never agreed to any test, the implied consent law says they did, simply by driving here.

lines.text: The driver is detained.
Taken to a hospital.
Staff may draw blood.

narration.text: What if an arrested driver refuses the breath test anyway? The manual is direct about it. A driver who refuses the breath test is detained and taken to a hospital, where staff may draw blood. So refusing does not end the matter or send the driver home. It moves the process to a hospital, and recall from the implied consent law that hospital staff are among those who can give the test. Refusal also brings its own penalties, which come next: a surcharge and, for a refusal conviction tied to a first offense, the loss of driving privileges until an ignition interlock device is installed. Refusing leads to detention, a possible blood draw and penalties of its own.

title.text: Refusal is not the cheap option

lines.text: Refusal surcharge: one thousand dollars a year, three years.
First DUI surcharge: the same amount and length.
First-offense refusal: no driving until interlock.

narration.text: Here is a trap. It is tempting to think that refusing the test avoids the money side of a DUI. The manual shows otherwise. Refusing a breath test carries a violation surcharge of one thousand dollars a year for three years. Compare that with a first DUI offense, which carries an annual surcharge of one thousand dollars for three years. The amounts and the length are the same. On top of that, a refusal conviction tied to a first offense means losing driving privileges until an ignition interlock device is installed. So a refusal brings the same yearly surcharge as a first DUI, plus a direct path to the interlock before driving again.

lines.text: Arrested, then refuses the test.
What happens, and what surcharge?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: Alex is arrested for intoxicated driving and refuses the breath test. What happens to Alex next, and what surcharge does the refusal carry? Work it out before reading on. Because of New Jersey's implied consent law, Alex already agreed to the test simply by driving on New Jersey roads. After refusing, Alex is detained and taken to a hospital, where staff may draw blood. The refusal carries a violation surcharge of one thousand dollars a year for three years. If the refusal conviction is tied to a first offense, Alex also loses driving privileges until an ignition interlock device is installed.

lines.text: Driving here means consenting.
Refusal: detention and a hospital.
One thousand dollars a year, three years.
No driving until an interlock.

narration.text: Here is the summary. Under New Jersey's implied consent law, simply driving on New Jersey roads means agreeing to a breath test by police or hospital staff after an arrest for intoxicated driving. A driver who refuses is detained and taken to a hospital, where staff may draw blood. Refusing carries a violation surcharge of one thousand dollars a year for three years, the same yearly amount and length as the first-DUI surcharge. And a refusal conviction tied to a first offense means losing driving privileges until an ignition interlock device is installed. The next unit explains how that interlock works and how long it must stay installed.

why_how.text: The interlock blocks the engine above zero point zero five percent, which is stricter than the adult limit of zero point zero eight.
After a first DUI the interlock term grows with BAC: three months, then seven months to one year, then the suspension plus twelve to fifteen months.

scenario.text: Robin's first DUI involved a BAC of zero point one zero to under zero point one five percent.

reasoning.text: That is the middle first-DUI tier, which requires the interlock for seven months to one year after restoration.

result.text: Robin keeps the interlock for seven months to one year after driving privileges are restored.

claim.text: Common mistake: assuming a refusal and a high-BAC first DUI carry the same interlock term.

correction.text: A refusal runs nine to fifteen months after restoration, while a high-BAC first DUI runs twelve to fifteen months after restoration.

memory_support.text: Point zero five blocks; three, seven, twelve.

prompt.text: Robin's first DUI involved a BAC of zero point one zero to under zero point one five percent. How long must the interlock stay after restoration?

answer.text: Seven months to one year after restoration.

rationale.text: The middle first-DUI tier requires seven months to one year, between the three months of the lowest tier and the twelve to fifteen months of the highest.

lines.text: A breathalyzer built into the car.
Terms depend on BAC and history.

narration.text: This unit is about the ignition interlock device, a tool New Jersey uses after DUI and refusal offenses. An ignition interlock device has a built-in breathalyzer that stops the vehicle from starting when the driver's BAC is above zero point zero five percent. The part to study closely is how long the device must stay installed, because the term changes with the BAC of a first DUI, with a refusal, and with a second or later offense. You will also learn about an option to install an interlock voluntarily before conviction, and what happens to a driver who ignores a court order to install one. The terms sit close together, so take them one at a time.

lines.text: Interlock blocks starts above zero point zero five.
Adult DUI limit: zero point zero eight.
The device line is lower.

narration.text: Start with how the device works. The interlock has a built-in breathalyzer, and it stops the vehicle from starting when the driver's BAC is above zero point zero five percent. Now compare that with the adult DUI limit, which is a BAC of zero point zero eight percent. The interlock blocks the engine once BAC tops just zero point zero five percent, so the device line is lower than the legal limit. That is the key contrast. A driver with an interlock can be under the adult DUI limit and still be unable to start the car. If a question asks about the interlock threshold, the answer is zero point zero five, not zero point zero eight.

lines.text: Zero point zero eight to under zero point one zero: three months.
Zero point one zero to under zero point one five: seven months to one year.
Counted from restoration of privileges.

narration.text: After a first DUI, the interlock term follows the BAC. After a first DUI with a BAC of zero point zero eight to under zero point one zero percent, the interlock stays installed for three months from restoration of driving privileges. After a first DUI with a BAC of zero point one zero to under zero point one five percent, the interlock is required for seven months to one year after restoration. Notice the starting point for both: the clock runs from restoration of driving privileges, not from the arrest. And notice the BAC boundaries, zero point one zero and zero point one five, because they decide which term applies. Lower tier, three months. Middle tier, seven months to one year.

lines.text: Zero point one five or higher: during suspension, then twelve to fifteen months.
Second or later offense: during suspension, then two to four years.

narration.text: Two terms are longer. After a first DUI at zero point one five percent or higher, the interlock is required during the suspension and for twelve to fifteen months after restoration. After a second or later DUI or refusal offense, the interlock is required during the suspension and for two to four years after restoration. Both of these name a feature the lower-tier terms do not mention: the interlock is required during the suspension itself, not only afterward. Then the terms after restoration differ sharply. Twelve to fifteen months for a high-BAC first offense, and two to four years for a repeat offense. Repeat offenses move the term from months into years.

lines.text: Refusal: nine to fifteen months after restoration.
High-BAC first DUI: twelve to fifteen months.
Same top, different bottom.

narration.text: Here is a pair that is easy to swap. For a breath-test refusal, the interlock runs for nine to fifteen months after restoration. For a first DUI at zero point one five percent or higher, it runs twelve to fifteen months after restoration. Both end at fifteen months, so the difference is the low end: nine for a refusal, twelve for a high-BAC first DUI. The high-BAC term also adds the time during the suspension. If you only remember fifteen, you will get both questions half right. Anchor the refusal to nine and the high BAC to twelve, and the shared fifteen at the top will take care of itself when you see either one in a question.

lines.text: On or after February nineteen, two thousand twenty-four.
Voluntary install before conviction may reduce penalties.
Skipping a court-ordered interlock adds one year.

narration.text: Two more rules complete the picture. First, for offenses on or after February nineteen, two thousand twenty-four, a person arrested for certain alcohol offenses may install an interlock voluntarily before conviction, which may reduce fines and the suspension period. The key words are voluntarily and before conviction, and the manual says may, not will. Second, the opposite situation: a driver who was ordered by a court to install an interlock and did not. Driving after failing to install a court-ordered interlock adds a one-year suspension on top of any existing suspension. One rule can soften the penalty for installing early; the other adds to it for not installing.

lines.text: First DUI, BAC zero point one zero to under zero point one five.
How long is the interlock?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: Robin's first DUI involved a BAC of zero point one zero to under zero point one five percent. How long must the interlock stay after restoration, and how would the answer change if Robin had refused the breath test instead? Work it out before reading on. For the middle first-DUI tier, the interlock is required for seven months to one year after restoration. For a breath-test refusal, the interlock runs nine to fifteen months after restoration. And remember the device itself: it stops the vehicle from starting when BAC is above zero point zero five percent, lower than the adult limit of zero point zero eight.

lines.text: Device blocks above zero point zero five.
Three months, seven months to a year, twelve to fifteen.
Refusal nine to fifteen; repeat two to four years.
Skip a court order: add one year.

narration.text: Let us lock in the interlock rules. The device stops the car from starting above zero point zero five percent, lower than the adult limit of zero point zero eight. After a first DUI, the term is three months for the lowest tier, seven months to one year for the middle tier, and the suspension plus twelve to fifteen months at zero point one five or higher. A refusal means nine to fifteen months, and a second or later offense means the suspension plus two to four years. For offenses on or after February nineteen, two thousand twenty-four, early voluntary installation may reduce penalties, and skipping a court-ordered interlock adds a one-year suspension.

narration.text: This unit covers what happens when someone drives while their license is suspended. The short version is that the penalties climb, both with each repeat offense and with the reason for the suspension. You will see the fines and jail terms for a first, second and third offense, then the tougher penalty when the suspension was for a DUI, a refusal or habitual offending. You will learn what changes when that driver goes near a school, when driving while suspended becomes a fourth-degree crime, and what an owner faces for knowingly handing the keys to a driver suspended for DUI or refusal. The numbers are close together, so take them one level at a time.

lines.text: First: five hundred dollars, up to six more months.
Second: seven hundred fifty dollars, up to five days in jail.
Third: one thousand dollars, ten-day jail term.

narration.text: Start with the ordinary case. Driving while suspended costs five hundred dollars plus up to six more months of suspension the first time. The second time, it costs seven hundred fifty dollars and up to five days in jail. The third time, it costs one thousand dollars with a ten-day jail term. Look at the pattern. The fine climbs from five hundred to seven hundred fifty to one thousand dollars. A jail term is listed starting with the second offense, as up to five days, and becomes a ten-day term at the third. The first offense is the one that adds up to six more months of suspension. Say the three levels in order and the pattern sticks.

lines.text: Suspended for DUI, refusal or habitual offending.
Five hundred dollar fine.
One to two more years of suspension.
Possible jail of ten to ninety days.

narration.text: The reason for the suspension matters. Driving while suspended for a DUI, a refusal or as a habitual offender brings a five hundred dollar fine and one to two more years of suspension, with possible jail of ten to ninety days. Compare that with an ordinary first offense, which adds up to six more months of suspension. The fine is the same five hundred dollars, but the added suspension jumps from months to one to two years, and possible jail of ten to ninety days is added. Recall that a habitual offender is a driver whose license has been suspended three times within three years. That label, like a DUI or a refusal, is what triggers this tougher penalty.

lines.text: School property, school crossing zone, or within one thousand feet.
One to two years of suspension, five hundred dollars.
Sixty to ninety days in jail.

narration.text: Here is where the jail ranges get confused. For a driver suspended for DUI, refusal or habitual offending, possible jail is ten to ninety days. But if that same suspended driver drives on school property, through a school crossing zone, or anywhere within one thousand feet of a school, the first-offense penalty is one to two years of suspension, a five hundred dollar fine and sixty to ninety days in jail. The suspension and the fine match the earlier rule. What changes is the jail term: the bottom of the range rises from ten days to sixty days. If a question mentions a school, a crossing zone or one thousand feet, think sixty to ninety days.

lines.text: Second or later DUI or refusal: fourth-degree crime.
An owner who knowingly lends the car is punished.
Up to six months of license and registration suspension.

narration.text: Two more rules extend the reach of these penalties. First, driving while suspended for a second or later DUI or refusal conviction is a fourth-degree crime. Keep that label tied to a second or later DUI or refusal conviction, not a first one. Second, the rules reach the owner of the car, not just the driver. An owner who knowingly lets someone drive whose license is suspended for DUI or refusal faces up to six months of license and registration suspension and a one thousand dollar fine, up to fifteen days in jail, or both. The key word is knowingly. An owner who hands the keys to a driver they know is suspended for DUI or refusal shares in the penalty.

The first offense would have been five hundred dollars plus up to six more months of suspension, and the third would be one thousand dollars with a ten-day jail term. If the suspension had been for a DUI, a refusal or habitual offending, the penalty would instead be a five hundred dollar fine, one to two more years of suspension and possible jail.

narration.text: Here is the wrap-up. Ordinary driving while suspended costs five hundred dollars plus up to six more months the first time, seven hundred fifty dollars and up to five days in jail the second, and one thousand dollars with a ten-day jail term the third. When the suspension was for a DUI, a refusal or habitual offending, it brings a five hundred dollar fine, one to two more years of suspension and possible jail of ten to ninety days, rising to sixty to ninety days near a school for a first offense. A second or later DUI or refusal suspension makes it a fourth-degree crime, and an owner who knowingly lends the car to such a driver faces penalties too.

narration.text: This unit turns to penalties for moving violations and a few rules about what happens inside the vehicle. You will start with unsafe driving, where fines climb with each offense, a court surcharge is added every time, and penalty points appear on a third or later offense within five years. Then you will see the penalty for a first reckless driving offense, the cost of failing to pass a vulnerable road user with due caution, and the places where fines double. Finally, you will cover open alcohol containers and unsealed cannabis items in the passenger area, and the fine for ignoring an officer's request to light up the compartment during a stop.

lines.text: First: fifty to one hundred fifty dollars.
Second: one hundred to two hundred fifty dollars.
Third or later: two hundred to five hundred dollars.
Plus a two hundred fifty dollar court surcharge.

narration.text: An unsafe driving conviction has three fine levels. The first time, the fine is fifty to one hundred fifty dollars. The second time, it is one hundred to two hundred fifty dollars. For a third or later offense, it is two hundred to five hundred dollars. Every time, there is also a two hundred fifty dollar court surcharge on top of the fine. Points enter the picture later. A third or later unsafe driving offense within five years of the previous one also adds four motor vehicle penalty points. So the surcharge comes with every conviction, while the four points depend on both the count and the timing: third or later, within five years of the last one.

lines.text: First reckless offense: up to sixty days in jail.
Fine of fifty to two hundred dollars, or both.
Vulnerable road user injured: five hundred dollars, two points.
No injury: one hundred dollars, no points.

narration.text: Reckless driving carries jail as an option. A first reckless driving offense can bring up to sixty days in jail, a fine of fifty to two hundred dollars, or both, and points are also assessed. Next, the rule for passing a vulnerable road user. Failing to pass a vulnerable road user with due caution is fined five hundred dollars with two penalty points if someone is injured, but one hundred dollars with no points if no one is hurt. Notice how the outcome of the pass changes the penalty. The same failure costs one hundred dollars and no points when no one is hurt, and five hundred dollars plus two penalty points when someone is injured.

lines.text: Highway construction zones: moving violation fines double.
Sixty-five zones: ten or more over doubles.
Certain other violations count too.

narration.text: Here is a pair that is easy to blur. Fines double for moving violations in highway construction zones. They also double in a sixty-five miles per hour zone, for speeding ten miles per hour or more over the limit or certain other moving violations. The trap is treating these as one rule. In a highway construction zone, the doubling applies to moving violations. In a sixty-five zone, the speeding trigger named is going ten miles per hour or more over the limit. So for speeding in a sixty-five zone, the manual sets the doubling line at ten miles per hour or more over. When a question names a work zone or a sixty-five zone, check which trigger it describes.

lines.text: Open container or unsealed cannabis: two hundred dollars first.
Later: two hundred fifty dollars or ten days of service.
Ignoring a request to light the compartment: fifty dollars.

narration.text: Two rules cover what happens inside the vehicle. Carrying an open or unsealed alcohol container, or an unsealed cannabis item, in the passenger area is fined two hundred dollars the first time. After that, the penalty is two hundred fifty dollars or ten days of community service. Notice that the rule covers cannabis as well as alcohol, and that it focuses on the passenger area. The second rule applies during a police stop. A driver who ignores a police officer's request to light up the driver's compartment during a stop faces a fifty dollar fine. Keep the two amounts apart: two hundred dollars for a first open container, fifty dollars for ignoring the lighting request.

What fine range applies, what surcharge is added, and does Morgan get any penalty points? Work it out before reading on. A third or later unsafe driving offense is fined two hundred to five hundred dollars. The two hundred fifty dollar court surcharge applies every time. And because this third offense came within five years of the previous one, it also adds four motor vehicle penalty points. Compare that with a first offense, which is fined fifty to one hundred fifty dollars plus the same two hundred fifty dollar court surcharge.

lines.text: Unsafe driving: fines climb, surcharge every time.
Reckless: up to sixty days in jail.

narration.text: Let us review. Unsafe driving is fined fifty to one hundred fifty dollars the first time, one hundred to two hundred fifty the second and two hundred to five hundred after that, plus a two hundred fifty dollar court surcharge each time, and a third or later offense within five years adds four points. A first reckless driving offense can bring up to sixty days in jail, a fifty to two hundred dollar fine, or both. Fines double in highway construction zones and in sixty-five zones for speeding ten or more over. An open container costs two hundred dollars the first time, and ignoring a request to light the compartment costs fifty.

lines.text: Snow, ice and abandoned vehicles.
Hit-and-run, fraud and boating DUI.

narration.text: This final unit gathers a set of offenses that each carry their own fines, jail terms or license losses. You will start with snow and ice, where a fine can apply even if nothing comes loose, and a larger fine applies when flying ice causes harm. Then you will see the penalties for leaving a vehicle on a limited-access highway, a hit-and-run involving injury or death, insurance fraud, lying on a license or registration application, and having someone else take your license test. Last comes boating, because a DUI on New Jersey waters reaches all of a person's driving privileges, not just the boat.

lines.text: Not clearing snow or ice: twenty-five to seventy-five dollars.
Flying ice causes harm: two hundred to one thousand dollars.
Commercial: five hundred to one thousand five hundred dollars.

narration.text: Snow and ice come with two levels of penalty. Failing to clear snow or ice from a vehicle before driving carries a twenty-five to seventy-five dollar fine even if none of it comes loose. So the offense is driving without clearing it, not only what happens afterward. If ice flies off a private vehicle and causes death, injury or property damage, the driver faces a fine of two hundred to one thousand dollars each time. For commercial owners and operators, the range is five hundred to one thousand five hundred dollars. Three ranges, then: the low one for not clearing at all, and two higher ones when flying ice causes harm, private and commercial.

lines.text: Four hours or more, without permission.
First: one hundred to five hundred dollars, up to two years.
Repeat: five hundred to one thousand dollars, up to five years.

narration.text: Leaving a vehicle on a limited-access highway is its own offense. Leaving a vehicle on or along a limited-access highway for four hours or more without permission brings a fine of one hundred to five hundred dollars and possible loss of driving privileges for up to two years. Do it again, and the penalty rises. Repeat vehicle abandonment raises the fine to five hundred to one thousand dollars with a suspension of up to five years. Two details define the offense: four hours or more, and without permission. Then the numbers step up together. The fine moves up to five hundred to one thousand dollars, and the license loss from up to two years to up to five.

lines.text: Hit-and-run with injury or death: fine, jail or both.
First offense: one-year license loss.
Later offense: permanent loss.
Boating DUI: boating and all driving privileges.

narration.text: Two serious offenses reach the license in a big way. A hit-and-run involving injury or death can bring a fine of two thousand five hundred to five thousand dollars, one hundred eighty days in jail, or both. On top of that comes a license loss: one year for a first offense and permanent loss for a later one. The second offense happens on water, not on the road. A boater convicted of DUI on New Jersey waters loses boating and all driving privileges, and a first offense is fined two hundred fifty to five hundred dollars. The connection is that both offenses cost driving privileges, even though one of them happens on the water instead of the road.

lines.text: Insurance fraud: up to five thousand dollars, three years.
Auto insurance crime: license lost for one year.
Lying on an application: up to six months in jail.

narration.text: Dishonesty on paper is penalized too. Insurance application or claim fraud can be punished by fines up to five thousand dollars, up to three years in prison, or both, and an auto insurance crime conviction also costs the license for one year. Lying on a license or registration application brings a two hundred to five hundred dollar fine, up to six months in jail, or both, and loss of license or registration privileges for six months to two years. Notice that both rules can cost driving privileges, not just money. Insurance fraud carries the larger fine and the longer possible prison term, while lying on an application costs privileges for six months to two years.

lines.text: Both: two hundred to five hundred dollars.
Stand-in license test: thirty to ninety days in jail.
Lying on an application: up to six months.

narration.text: Here is a pair that shares a fine and splits on jail. Having someone else take your license test, or taking it for someone else, brings a two hundred to five hundred dollar fine, thirty to ninety days in jail, or both. Lying on a license or registration application brings the same two hundred to five hundred dollar fine, but with up to six months in jail, or both. Because the fines match, the jail term is the detail that separates them. Note also that the stand-in rule punishes both sides: the person who has someone else take the test and the person who takes it for them. Fine alike, jail different, and both the applicant and the stand-in are covered.

narration.text: Here is a quick check: Nico skipped clearing the car after a storm, and on the highway a sheet of ice flies off and damages another vehicle. Nico drives a private car, not a commercial vehicle. What fine can Nico face for the flying ice, and what would the fine have been if nothing had come loose? Work it out before reading on. When ice flies off a private vehicle and causes property damage, the driver faces a fine of two hundred to one thousand dollars each time. If none of the snow or ice had come loose, failing to clear it would still carry a twenty-five to seventy-five dollar fine. Commercial owners and operators face five hundred to one thousand five hundred dollars.

lines.text: Snow not cleared: twenty-five to seventy-five dollars.
Abandonment: up to two years, repeat up to five.
Hit-and-run: one year, then permanent.
Boating DUI costs all driving privileges.

narration.text: Let us close the lesson. Failing to clear snow or ice is fined twenty-five to seventy-five dollars even if none comes loose, and flying ice that causes harm costs a private driver two hundred to one thousand dollars. Abandoning a vehicle on a limited-access highway risks up to two years of lost privileges, and a repeat risks up to five. A hit-and-run involving injury or death brings a one-year license loss for a first offense and permanent loss for a later one. Insurance fraud, lying on an application and a stand-in license test each carry fines and possible jail, and a boater convicted of DUI on New Jersey waters loses all driving privileges.
